text.en: Kavya draws a bean plant on Monday and again on Thursday. The pot has not moved, but the shoot in her second drawing curves nearer to the window. She circles the growing tip and wonders what that change can tell her.

Track the root and shoot tips to see changes in a bean seedling. Compare upright and inverted seedlings to investigate starting position. Compare two upright seedlings with different lighting to investigate the direction of light.
A bean plant sits in one place, yet its shoot bends toward a window. The shoot has changed position as it grew. Movement can happen in part of a plant without the whole plant moving away.
Look at a young bean seedling. The first root extends from the bean. A shoot grows from the seedling and later carries leaves. We can track root and shoot separately.
Make a sketch on the first day. Draw the bean and mark the positions of the root tip and shoot tip. Use the tips as landmarks in later sketches.
In the next sketch, look for two kinds of change. A tip farther from the seed can be evidence of growth. A changed direction is evidence of movement as the plant grows.

board.text: A bend shows a change in direction

text.en: We will compare three drawings of an investigation. Each shows a similar bean seedling with a small root and shoot. Line them up so we can compare their starting conditions.
The seedlings in the drawings rest on damp supports above the water. Each has a supply of moisture and access to air. Make the supports and water levels similar in all three.

board.text: Same moisture and access to air

text.en: Put the first seedling upright in our model. Place it where light is available from more than one side. This seedling gives us a starting point for both comparisons.

board.text: A: upright, light from several sides

text.en: Turn the second seedling upside down. Before new growth, its root tip points up and its shoot tip points down. It receives light in the same way as the first seedling.

board.text: B: inverted, same lighting as A

text.en: The third seedling starts upright. An opening on one side lets light reach the shoot from that side. This differs from the lighting for the first seedling.

board.text: C: upright, light from one side

text.en: Compare A and B. Their lighting is similar and their starting positions differ. This pair can help us test whether turning the seedling changes where the tips grow.

board.text: Compare A and B to test starting position

text.en: Compare A and C. Both are upright at the start. Their lighting differs, so we can compare how the shoots grow when light comes from different directions.

board.text: Compare A and C to test light direction

text.en: Make a prediction before you look at the later drawings. Add an arrow where you expect each root and shoot tip to grow. Your prediction gives you something to check against observations.

board.text: Mark a prediction before seeing results

text.en: Check A first. The new root growth extends downward. The new shoot growth extends upward. The later drawing shows the tips farther from the seed.

board.text: A later: root down, shoot up

text.en: Check the inverted seedling B. The older part of the root still points up from the seed. Trace it to the bend, then follow the new growth downward.

board.text: B root: starts up, bends down

text.en: Check the shoot in B. The older part points down from the seed, but the new growth curves upward. Look at the direction at the tip to see the change.

board.text: B shoot: starts down, bends up

text.en: Why use one drawing from the start and one from later? The early one shows how the seedling was placed. The later one shows the direction of the new growth.
Gravity provides a direction cue. In this comparison the roots in A and B both grow downward even though the seedlings were placed in different positions.
Now check C. Follow its shoot tip to the side with the opening. New shoot growth bends toward the light in our drawing.

board.text: C shoot bends toward the opening

text.en: Look below the bean in C. The root is still growing downward. In this comparison the root and shoot show different responses.
Imagine moving the opening to the opposite side with a similar seedling. Predict where you would sketch the shoot tip after more growing time. Keep the other conditions similar.

board.text: New prediction: reverse the direction of light

text.en: A stimulus is a change or clue in the surroundings that a living thing can respond to. The direction of light is a clue for the shoot. Its bend is an observable response.

board.text: Response: shoot bends as it grows

text.en: The same plant can make other kinds of movement. Some leaves fold when touched. The bean shoot in our comparison bends gradually as it grows over time.

board.text: Bean shoot bending takes growing time

text.en: A good record names the seedling and includes the date and direction of the sketch. Mark which side the light came from so someone else can read the record later.

board.text: Record the date, seedling and light direction

text.en: Draw a small arrow for down beside each sketch. Then you can tell whether the page was turned when it was viewed. A fixed arrow helps us compare each root accurately.

board.text: Keep a down arrow on each sketch

text.en: Keep the same kind of seedling and make the moisture levels similar. If a seedling dries out, its movement may be harder to interpret. Write down any unusual change you notice.
An observation describes what you saw. The shoot tip moved closer to the opening is an observation. Light direction influenced the shoot is a conclusion from comparing the drawings.
One plant may grow unevenly or be damaged. If you can observe several comparable plants, check how many show the same bend before drawing a conclusion.
The Indian scientist Jagadish Chandra Bose made an instrument that could record tiny changes as plants grew. The instrument was called a crescograph.
At home you may see a potted plant leaning toward the brightest part of a room. Make a sketch from the same place on two dates and look for new growth before deciding what happened.

board.text: Use the same viewpoint for both sketches

text.en: Explain one comparison aloud. Name the two seedlings, say what differed at the start, and point to the tip that changed its direction. Finish with what that observation supports.

problem.en: Which drawings would you compare to test whether light from one side changes the direction of shoot growth?

text.en: Compare the two seedlings that both started upright.

why.en: Starting position stays the same in this comparison.

text.en: Identify which seedling received light from one side through the opening.

why.en: The direction of the light is the condition that differs here.

text.en: Compare the later shoot tips and explain the difference you can see.

why.en: A bend toward the opening is evidence that shoot growth responded to the direction of the light.

prompt.en: Explain how to tell the difference between the position of an inverted bean seedling and the direction of its new root growth.

requiredIdeas.en: The inverted root starts by pointing up.
The growing tip later bends downward.
Compare a start sketch with a later sketch.

commonMisconceptions.en: The initial position shows the direction of all later growth.

points.en: Use root and shoot tips to track plant growth.
The root of an inverted bean seedling can bend downward as it grows.
An upright shoot can bend toward light from one side.
Change one condition at a time in a comparison.
